title: Can unhelpful beliefs actually be useful?
description: This article explores how unhelpful beliefs affect your mental well-being. Using the example of John, who strives for success due to a core belief of inadequacy, we see how such beliefs can turn into unhelpful coping strategies. The author emphasizes the importance of noticing and re-examining your beliefs to improve your quality of life.

texts: In previous chapters, we’ve focused heavily on unhelpful thoughts and beliefs. This makes sense: they are the ones that significantly impact your emotions, behavior, and overall well-being.
This raises a question: are all beliefs harmful, or can some of them actually be helpful?
Most often, unhelpful beliefs are triggered by stressful situations, low moods, or depression, as well as by events that seem to confirm them.
For example, if someone holds the belief “I am incapable,” it will likely be triggered after failing an exam or receiving criticism from a boss.
The person then begins to view everything through the lens of that belief, even if that perspective is illogical or doesn’t align with the facts.
However, this doesn’t mean that all beliefs are equally bad or useless.
In less stressful circumstances or when you’re feeling more resilient, a helpful belief might “switch on,” such as: “I am capable enough.”
So, to answer the question “Are all beliefs harmful?” — the answer is no, not all of them.
When it comes to the “usefulness” of unhelpful beliefs, things are more complex than they appear at first glance — let’s dive in.
It might sometimes seem like these beliefs drive achievement, but this is more of a common misconception than a reality.
To clarify, let’s recall the three levels: automatic thoughts, intermediate beliefs, and core beliefs.
Imagine a young man named John who has a core belief: “I am incapable,” and an intermediate belief: “I must always be successful.”
On one hand, it sounds okay: striving for success is a worthy goal if it’s a flexible desire rather than a rigid rule.
You might think such a belief is helpful, as if it would boost motivation, drive achievement, and increase purpose.
In this view, work seems incredibly important and appears to bring only benefits.
But let’s look deeper.

If this is truly a rigid intermediate belief rather than just a desire, it will likely prove to be unhelpful because it is rooted in a core belief of inadequacy. In this case, work becomes a coping strategy for John (we’ll discuss coping strategies in future chapters).
<q author="Leo Tolstoy">Since a person can only love or hate their work, they must see its consequences. Workaholics simply forget that they do not exist for work, but work exists for them.</q>
In short: a coping strategy is a way of responding to stress through your thoughts, feelings, or behavior.

<important>To put it simply, John strives to be successful (an intermediate belief) so that he doesn’t have to feel “incapable” (a core belief). Focusing on work becomes a way to avoid a painful sense of self.</important>

This is unhelpful because any significant setback at work — a failed project, a career delay, or a job loss — can sharply trigger John’s core belief of inadequacy, which feels like an “internal apocalypse.”
The consequences include worsening mental well-being, apathy, self-destructive behavior, and even depression.
Now, those potential “benefits” don’t look so convincing, do they?
It turns out the belief “I must always be successful” is actually unhelpful: mistakes are inevitable, and with such rigidity, every mistake will “prove” his inadequacy and reinforce it even further.

It’s important to remember: a belief is just an idea that can be re-examined and made more helpful. This significantly improves your quality of life — and that is exactly what cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) teaches you.
